i know many players have reservations about ai-generated content, so i want to be upfront about exactly how it was used in this game. i'm an ordinary gamer who has played games for almost twenty years and always dreamed of making one of my own. but i can't write code, and i've never been trained in art or music. this game exists because generative ai filled those gaps for me: parts of the code were written with the help of ai coding tools; some character, environment, and ui art was created with image-generation models, then hand-picked and adjusted by me; some animation, music, and sound effects were also made with ai tools. everything that makes it an actual game, though — the design, the balancing, the game feel, and every "is this fun?" decision — was done by me, across hundreds of playtests. the game contains no live-generated ai content. for me, ai wasn't an assembly line making a game in my place. it's what let an ordinary player finally build the game he'd been dreaming about. i hope some of that comes through when you play — and i'd genuinely welcome your feedback.

we're just a small team who loves making games and we love using ai to make them even better. we know there’s been a lot of negativity around ai in games lately, and honestly, we get it. but for us, ai isn’t some big scary thing, it’s a tool we use every day with excitement and care. it helps us bring our world to life, and gives players new ways to express their own creativity. in our game, ai is used to make things feel more alive. it helps players voice their characters, translate their stories for others to enjoy around the world, and build cool things they might not have been able to otherwise. we're not using ai to replace artists or writers, we're using it to give more people the power to create. we believe in giving players tools, not walls. ai is one of those tools, and we're constantly working to use it in thoughtful, respectful ways that fit our vision and our values. so if you're on the fence about ai in games, we just ask: give it a chance. we’re doing our best to make something special here. this game is built with love, and we hope that shows in every part of it, even the parts powered by ai.

this project was initiated in september 2022. as part of an academic exploration of emerging technologies, ai image generation tools (which were still in the early stages of development at the time) were used to assist with the visual processing of certain content, and an ai music generation tool was used in the production of the background music. to avoid the misuse of generative ai tools, only the default datasets provided by the respective tools were used during development. the methods of use included: 1. processing real photographs to create "alien" or "distorted" visual effects; 2. using abstract images generated from provided keywords as references for manual redesign, reconstruction, and painting; 3. generating atmospheric music clips by adjusting parameters such as instrumentation and tempo, followed by manual editing and refinement. all content involving artificial intelligence was completed before 2023. since then, the use of ai image generation technology in development has been fully discontinued and will not continue in future production. for all ai-generated image assets used in this work, only usage rights are retained by the project.

as the ai debate continues to evolve i feel the need to add nuance to this statement so players can make an informed decision whether or not to support human game developers. i took 5 years of classes learning code and 3d to produce my game. when the ai boom hit, tobiano was already a functioning breeding and management simulator. at my day job, we were encouraged to use ai for everything from image generation to writing emails. i opposed the use of ai for creative aspects and human communication, but tested out chatbots for help with code. problems solved with ai include things like "how do i make the camera follow the player". a lot of the problems ended up more convoluted by ai. most of the code written early in the game has gone through 2-3 iterations to simplify and be easier to work with and debug. for example, the riding lesson system was redone completely after the first 5 lessons were added, just to make the next 5 lessons easier for me to add. building a large and complex game requires understanding of code and the developer needs to know where to find every method, every variable. there is an important distinction between "hey claude, build me a horse game" and saving a couple hours writing a database. i've spent literally thousands of hours writing code for my passion project. ai use in the game today consists of time-saving things like "add these markings to this list". ai can be useful for debugging, when the root of a problem can be a simple typo that is hard to spot. bigger debugging problems always require a broader conceptual understanding of the way the game is set up and take human hours to solve. ai has not been used to create any 3d assets, textures, audio, or writing or translations in the game. i cannot guarantee that people i hire to do these tasks do not use ai, as these cooperations are based on trust. my discord community see behind the scenes and know the care and work that goes into this game. as time goes on i take the gamble that my efforts will produce something that players can enjoy, knowing they are supporting human game developers.

equilibrium uses generative ai to power its core gameplay mechanic: the policy terminal. live-generated content when a player types a directive or law in natural language (e.g., "abolish the luxury car tax"), the ai engine analyzes the request in real time and generates a structured governmental dossier, including: - legislative feasibility analysis - budget impact and financial coverage - macroeconomic effects (gdp, debt, inflation) - social and political consensus projections - parliamentary vote simulation model used: anthropic claude, accessed via api. guardrails: ai output is constrained to a fixed set of structured fields defined by the developer. all numeric effects are clamped within bounds enforced by the simulation engine, so no ai output can produce values outside the game's defined ranges. the model operates only on the simulation state provided to it and cannot invent game data: commands that cannot be mapped to a valid government action are refused, and the player is offered bounded policy alternatives instead. no image, audio, or user-data generation is involved, and no player data is used to train any model. because responses are generated at runtime, outputs vary between playthroughs: the same directive may produce different wording and different outcomes. pre-generated content the game's background music track was generated using ai tools during development and ships with the game.

dead reckoning is written, and designed by one person. i want to be precise about where ai tools do and don't appear in it. creative content — no generative ai. all writing, narrative, and design is mine. i've worked as a technical writer for twelve years; the game's voice is my own. all art and visual assets are hand-made or licensed from named human artists. all music and sound effects are licensed from named human creators (public domain / creative commons) — none of it is ai-generated. this is a hard line and i intend to keep it. development & release tooling — where ai assists. i use ai in the engineering and release pipeline only, never to author the game itself: - coding assistance while writing the game's gdscript. - an automated qa/test harness that plays the simulation thousands of times to catch crashes and balance regressions. - assistance in building linters (valve yaml sheets) that check the project's text. - drafting and summarizing the release notes (patch notes) from the project's changelog. none of this creates any of the writing, art, audio, or design inside the game. localization. the four translations (german, french, italian, spanish) are machine-translated by deepl from my english source, with automated guards that fall back to english wherever a translation would break. this is an accessibility vs. quality decision, and i decided on the former. proper localizations are planned and will be contracted out if the budget allows.

# ai usage in our game in our game, we have utilized generative artificial intelligence (ai) technology to enhance certain aspects of the visual experience. specifically, we have employed ai-powered tools to assist in the creation of some background images and textures. key points about our ai usage: 1. **pre-rendered content**: the ai-generated elements are pre-rendered during the development process. this means that the images you see in the game are not being created in real-time as you play. 2. **limited scope**: ai has been used primarily for non-essential background elements and textures. all main characters, story-critical environments, and core gameplay elements are hand-crafted by our artists. 3. **human oversight**: while ai tools have been used to generate initial ideas or base images, our art team carefully reviews, edits, and refines all ai-assisted content to ensure it meets our quality standards and fits seamlessly into the game's aesthetic. 4. **no live generation**: our game does not use ai to generate any content during gameplay. all ai-assisted elements are fixed and do not change dynamically. 5. **copyright compliance**: we have taken great care to ensure that all ai-generated content is original and does not infringe on existing copyrights. our use of ai tools is in compliance with their terms of service and licensing agreements. we believe that the thoughtful use of ai in our development process has allowed us to create richer, more detailed environments for players to explore, while maintaining the artistic integrity and vision of our game. as always, we welcome player feedback and are committed to providing a high-quality gaming experience.

all of the images in this game are generated by neural networks trained on images (aka “ai generated”). if you choose to boycott all ai generated material, please do not buy this game. if you are uncomfortable with the thought but are interested in my game, please read on. the aesthetic of this game had to come from the strange, uncanny look of ai. there is a heartlessness to the visuals that is intentional. i am not trying to copy the look of other artists. the only tool capable of producing the look i was going for was a malfunctioning ai. ironically, i have had a number of people tell me that it looks much more realistic than standard ai. i am assuming this is because of how i tried to reproduce the look of old media. all images, aside from the title screen, credits and some of the video shot on camcorder were generated by ai prompts. it took several days of exploring before i began generating images that fit the aesthetic i was looking for. i have heard ai described as a slot machine, and i think the metaphor is somewhat accurate. i think of this as similar to indeterminacy in music. using random number generators can produce interesting outputs, but you need to refine and direct the system to do so. i started my process in midjourney. my ratio of usable images was around 100 to 1; for every 100 images i generated, i found one usable piece for the game. i created an automated process to transform these images to 16:9 widescreen in photoshop beta. some of these images i touched up manually or regenerated sections of the image. there are some real images and hand painted imagery within the ai elements. often, i would have to generate the sides of the image multiple times because photoshop didn’t generate what i needed. to those concerned about not paying artists: i understand this, but i want to be clear that this was not created to replace the work of artists, any more than the synthesized scores to horror films were about replacing orchestras. these are tools that do different things. rather than some sort of lazy shortcut, the use of ai imagery is essential to the aesthetic and narrative of the path of veins.

hi everyone. i want to be open about how this game was made and why generative ai was used. aika was supposed to die began as a story that i wrote and developed over more than two years. the world, characters, dialogue, themes, and narrative direction were all written by me. i cared deeply about this story, and eventually i felt that a visual novel would be the best way to bring it to life. as an independent developer working with a limited budget, hiring a full team of artists is not financially possible for me right now. i greatly value human-made art and the work of professional artists. i am also a 3d artist who works with unreal engine, so this is something i genuinely care about. rather than leave the story untold, i chose to use generative ai as part of the visual production process. the game’s images and video assets were created with the assistance of generative ai tools. however, i did not want that to become an excuse for delivering something careless or low-quality. in fact, having access to these tools encouraged me to be as ambitious as possible with the project. i created and refined a large number of images and animated sequences to give the game a richer and more cinematic presentation. every asset was carefully directed, selected, edited, revised, and manually integrated into the story, with the goal of providing players with a cohesive, polished, and emotionally engaging experience. the writing, narrative design, scene direction, timing, editing, and final creative decisions were all handled by humans. generative ai was used as a production tool, not as a replacement for authorship, creative direction, or care. no ai content is generated during gameplay. if the game becomes successful enough to support a larger production, i would love to work with professional artists on future chapters. until then, this approach has allowed me to share a story that means a great deal to me while doing everything within my reach to make the final experience cohesive, personal, and emotionally meaningful. thank you for giving this story a chance.

our policy for ai use even if, and disclose from time to time that, we use ai in some of our products, it never means that our product consists of ai-generated content, which is simply impossible but may be presumed by some people. we continue our due diligence and necessary efforts to come up with the best content. ai is a field that we keep track of and welcome curiously and excitedly. it is something not the world gives us but what we get from the world according to our requirements. however, we always consider the rights of commercial and ethical use of ai. therefore, we subscribe to their content, pay their respective fee, and keep their receipts/licenses. how may we use ai? we may use outsourced ai in a number of different ways in addition to our own in-game ai mechanics, as it gives us uniqueness and originality as we like, and as long as its content is compliant with our above policy: sound files: we have a large collection of audio clips we have purchased and keep purchasing. we also have the means to make our own sound files. sometimes we may also use ai-made sounds to make audio clips as well if we fail to find what we are looking for in our archive. graphics: we may use ai for some of our graphical assets. we have various means like software with which we can create characters, particularly our animated characters in the trailers and cutscenes, which are our own unique designs. we may use ai in this particular game in relation to the environment and some of the ancillary icons, finishings, and corrections. ideas: we may chat with ai about whether an idea is suitable for the current genre we are working on. however, we plan to discontinue this use of ai as it lacks originality. for example, when we asked for the names of two female characters for a fantasy game, ai suggested “anya and ayleen.” they are obviously names used before and we needed to change the names of our two characters. the above use of our ai may naturally appear on our store page as we include fragments from our game to introduce and promote it. this policy may be subject to change depending on the developments, ethical considerations, and circumstances regarding the use of ai in the future.

i use a highly curated ai prompt, driven by automation software, to generate levels for the game. by taking an ai prompt that describes the basic architecture of a level, and adding the difficulty and a theme description, i get back an 8x20 grid. i then run a post process bit of code that looks for errors, and re-generates the level if an error is found. i also use a highly curated ai prompt, driven by automation software, to generate new avatars. again, i add a theme (e.g. cute baby animals dressed as pirates) plus a list of about 260 animals to generate the base avatars. i then run image processing to remove the background and create a variety of sizes. finally, i look at each avatar individually and edit to finalize removal of the background if anything was missed, or even redo the background removal manually if it got messed up by the automated image processor.

scourge of the necromancer makes significant use of generative ai in its production. we want to be fully upfront about it. visual assets (2d images + video) — all ai-generated, then human-curated and human-edited. every shipped image and video in the game and on the steam store page was produced with ai tools, then reviewed, edited, and selected by hand by the developer. this covers: steam store capsules and library art, the store-page background, all in-game achievement icons, hero portraits, the necromancer concept art, decorative ui elements, all real-time cinematics (the defeat sequence and all victory variants), and the marketing trailer's atmospheric segments. image models used: google imagen 4, google veo 3.1 (video), nano banana pro / gemini 3 pro image (google), black forest labs flux.2, recraft v4 pro, ideogram v3, and bria rmbg-2.0 (background removal). final assets received human editing — compositing, color correction, retouching, frame extraction, masking, and rejection of unusable outputs. 3d models — ai-generated base meshes, then human-edited in blender. the in-game hero character models (knight, cleric, ranger, wizard, warrior, alchemist) started as outputs from tripo ai's generative 3d model service (fbx + texture pngs), but each model was then opened in blender by the developer for hand editing — mesh cleanup, geometry adjustments, and texture fixes — before being exported for use in the game. each finished model was imported into unity with hand-tuned scale, rotation, material configuration, and import-setting curation. unsatisfactory generations were discarded and re-prompted; the blender editing step is substantial enough that the shipped models are not pure ai output. music — ai-generated, then human-curated and post-processed. all music tracks in the game (menu, gameplay layers, boss phases, victory, defeat) were produced with google gemini's music generation, then human-selected, trimmed, looped, and mixed by the developer. necromancer voice — ai-generated, then human-edited. the necromancer's spoken syllables were synthesized with elevenlabs text-to-speech (eleven multilingual v2 model), then pitch-shifted, eq'd, and processed with reverb in audacity by the developer to produce the final in-game delivery. no other character has spoken voice lines in the shipped game. sound effects — all ai-generated. every sfx in the game (ability sounds, ambient layers, ui sounds, footsteps, kill/spawn cues, tile state cues, boss audio) was produced with elevenlabs sound effects, then human-selected, trimmed, processed, and mixed by the developer. the necromancer voice lines use elevenlabs text-to-speech (covered separately above). runtime behavior. the game does not use live-generated ai content at runtime. every shipped asset is a fixed, pre-rendered file. player-facing text, dialogue, narrative, lore, and game design were written by the developer without ai generation. code. code development used claude (anthropic) as an ai coding assistant. this is behind-the-scenes efficiency tooling not consumed by players, but we mention it here for full transparency.

to learn gdscript and build every system in the game. the first line in my prompts is always "stop being a yes sayer and always be brutal and honest." here is exactly what ai was and wasn't used for: code: i spent my first three months writing every line of code by hand. as the project grew, ai became a development partner — drafting code from my descriptions, which i then reviewed, debugged, and ai is used to generate the voices and advice of two opposing royal advisers (left and right councillor). each turn they comment on the situation and recommend different actions. if the player’s decree aligns more closely with one adviser’s stance, that adviser’s credibility increases while the other’s decreases. as the credibility gap grows, public trust is affected, reflecting rising factional tension. if an adviser’s credibility reaches zero, they resign—sometimes angrily—warning the player not to dismiss their counsel. the vacant seat is then filled by a successor adviser, represented by a different local llm model. this creates shifting personalities and advice styles across runs. ai does not determine the game’s outcomes. core consequences and metric changes are resolved by the game’s rule system; ai provides narrative and guidance within that system.
